newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ teenager debunks "Noddy" myths with maths.
newsitem.headline: NZ teenager debunks "Noddy" myths with maths.

text.p: A 14-year-old New Zealand boy has won a mathematics competition with a statistical analysis of the classic "Noddy" children's books in which he shows that contemporary allegations of political incorrectness lack foundation.

British author Enid Blyton's illustrated books about Noddy and his friends in Toytown have been read by children around the world for the last 60 years, but since the 1980s they have been hit by adult accusations of racism, sexism and masochism.
The boy, Tom Hallett-Hook, said on Thursday he dug out his collection of all 23 original Noddy books and conducted a study called "Was Noddy Framed?", as his entry in the Mathex '97 competition.

He found black gollywogs were hardly ever villains, while Noddy often was, while Tessie Bear was full of initiative -- contrary to allegations that she failed to provide an assertive female role model -- and the milkman only hit Noddy three times.
Concerns that words and attitudes in some of the books might offend modern sensitivities had encouraged publishers to revise the characters in 1992, before a television series was made.
But Hallett-Hook decided to dissect the original series and seek out data that would support the revisionists' claims.
At the end of his analysis he concluded: "Noddy was framed".

"First I read through all the Noddy books and looked for instances of, say, gollywogs being good or bad...and Tessie Bear taking initiative or not, and went through them all and plotted them all on charts," he told New Zealand Radio.
Asked if golliwogs were naughty, Hallett-Hook said: "No, they weren't. I found that of all the villains in Noddy, only six percent of them were golliwog ones".
"The naughtiest character has to be Noddy himself".
Studying the behaviour of Noddy's friend Tessie Bear, who was alleged not be assertive enough, he found much more evidence to the contrary that she was positive and forward-thinking.

And when examining the basis for claims that the milkman was portraying masochistic tendencies by asking to hit Noddy on the head instead of being paid, the young statistician said the numbers didn't stack up and Blyton had been clear about pain.
"We found that he only bangs Noddy on the head about three times in all the books overall. Also, Noddy's head was made out of wood and they explained that it didn't hurt in the books," he added.
The student's investigation was chosen for the overall prize out of more than one thousand entries from across Auckland.
